- Route all traffic back to stable: set Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0
- Or scale canary to 0: kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns scale deploy/engine-v2-1 --replicas=0

Steps.message:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The Deployment overrode the container command with /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing CrashLoopBackOff (/bin/sh: 1: nonexistent_command: not found).
- Change made: Updated Deployment crashloop-test/app to run nginx properly:
  - command: ["nginx"]
  - args: ["-g", "daemon off;"]
- Current state: 1/1 replicas available, Pod app-784bb86f68-s8hdp is Running.

If you’d prefer to use the image’s default entrypoint instead, I can remove command/args entirely.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The Deployment overrode the container command with /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing CrashLoopBackOff (/bin/sh: 1: nonexistent_command: not found).
- Change made: Updated Deployment crashloop-test/app to run nginx properly:
  - command: ["nginx"]
  - args: ["-g", "daemon off;"]
- Current state: 1/1 replicas available, Pod app-784bb86f68-s8hdp is Running.

If you’d prefer to use the image’s default entrypoint instead, I can remove command/args entirely.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

- Root cause: The Deployment was using a non-existent image tag quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag, causing ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff.
- Change made: Updated the container image to quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest in Deployment debug/app.
- Result: The Deployment is healthy.
  - Pod: app-7db8cc5485-k5v7x is Running (1/1).
  - Deployment status: Available=True, replicas=1/1, progressing successfully.

If you prefer a pinned version instead of latest, tell me the desired tag and I’ll update it (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:<specific-version>).

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What happened:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the PVC couldn’t bind and the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed:
- Recreated the PVC with storageClassName: standard (the default available in your cluster).

Result:
- A volume was provisioned and bound to the PVC.
- The pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.

If you prefer a different StorageClass, tell me which one and I can update the PVC accordingly.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

What happened:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the PVC couldn’t bind and the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed:
- Recreated the PVC with storageClassName: standard (the default available in your cluster).

Result:
- A volume was provisioned and bound to the PVC.
- The pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.

If you prefer a different StorageClass, tell me which one and I can update the PVC accordingly.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What happened:
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the PVC couldn’t bind and the pod couldn’t schedule.

What I changed:
- Recreated the PVC with storageClassName: standard (the default available in your cluster).

Result:
- A volume was provisioned and bound to the PVC.
- The pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns is now Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster.

If you prefer a different StorageClass, tell me which one and I can update the PVC accordingly.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Health probes were checking port 80 on paths /get_status and /is_ready (which don’t exist on the stock nginx image).
  - The Service was targeting port 80.
- This caused liveness/readiness probe failures and restarts (CrashLoopBackOff).

What I changed
- Updated Deployment webapp (namespace: orders):
  - Liveness/Readiness probes now GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated Service webapp:
  - targetPort set to 8080 (Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Running.
- Deployment is Available (1/1).
- Service points to the healthy pod.

How to verify
- Port-forward and curl:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - curl -I http://localhost:8080
  - You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK from nginx.

If you actually need custom health endpoints (/get_status, /is_ready), I can add an nginx config to serve those or switch to the correct app image.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Health probes were checking port 80 on paths /get_status and /is_ready (which don’t exist on the stock nginx image).
  - The Service was targeting port 80.
- This caused liveness/readiness probe failures and restarts (CrashLoopBackOff).

What I changed
- Updated Deployment webapp (namespace: orders):
  - Liveness/Readiness probes now GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated Service webapp:
  - targetPort set to 8080 (Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Running.
- Deployment is Available (1/1).
- Service points to the healthy pod.

How to verify
- Port-forward and curl:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - curl -I http://localhost:8080
  - You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK from nginx.

If you actually need custom health endpoints (/get_status, /is_ready), I can add an nginx config to serve those or switch to the correct app image.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The container image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Health probes were checking port 80 on paths /get_status and /is_ready (which don’t exist on the stock nginx image).
  - The Service was targeting port 80.
- This caused liveness/readiness probe failures and restarts (CrashLoopBackOff).

What I changed
- Updated Deployment webapp (namespace: orders):
  - Liveness/Readiness probes now GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080.
- Updated Service webapp:
  - targetPort set to 8080 (Service still exposes port 80 inside the cluster).

Current status
- Pod is healthy: 1/1 Running.
- Deployment is Available (1/1).
- Service points to the healthy pod.

How to verify
- Port-forward and curl:
  - kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80
  - curl -I http://localhost:8080
  - You should see HTTP/1.1 200 OK from nginx.

If you actually need custom health endpoints (/get_status, /is_ready), I can add an nginx config to serve those or switch to the correct app image.

Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup only granted list on apps/deployments and did not grant any permissions on core/pods. So the pod-reader service account had no right to list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role pod-reader-role to include permissions on pods:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Left the existing deployments list permission intact.
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already binds the service account simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to this Role, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- Run: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Or: kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

You should now be able to list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace with the pod-reader service account.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Role pod-reader-role in simple-rbac-setup only granted list on apps/deployments and did not grant any permissions on core/pods. So the pod-reader service account had no right to list pods.

What I fixed
- Updated the Role pod-reader-role to include permissions on pods:
  - apiGroup: "" (core)
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- Left the existing deployments list permission intact.
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already binds the service account simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to this Role, so no change was needed there.

How to verify
- Run: kubectl -n simple-rbac-setup get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- Or: kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

You should now be able to list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace with the pod-reader service account.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels. Service web/nginx had selector app=web, while the nginx Deployment/Pod is labeled app=nginx. This left the Service with no endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach the Pod.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to app=nginx.
- Result: Endpoints are now populated: nginx → 10.244.0.25:8080, and the Pod is Ready (1/1).

Current state
- Service: ClusterIP 10.108.206.205:80, selector app=nginx, targetPort 8080.
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.25:8080 (healthy).
- This should now be accessible from inside the cluster.

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- From another pod:
  - kubectl -n web run curl --image=curlimages/curl --rm -it --restart=Never -- curl -sSI http://nginx
- Or by ClusterIP:
  - kubectl -n web run curl --image=curlimages/curl --rm -it --restart=Never -- curl -sSI http://10.108.206.205

If you need external access

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Root cause
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels. Service web/nginx had selector app=web, while the nginx Deployment/Pod is labeled app=nginx. This left the Service with no endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach the Pod.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to app=nginx.
- Result: Endpoints are now populated: nginx → 10.244.0.25:8080, and the Pod is Ready (1/1).

Current state
- Service: ClusterIP 10.108.206.205:80, selector app=nginx, targetPort 8080.
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.25:8080 (healthy).
- This should now be accessible from inside the cluster.

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- From another pod:
  - kubectl -n web run curl --image=curlimages/curl --rm -it --restart=Never -- curl -sSI http://nginx
- Or by ClusterIP:
  - kubectl -n web run curl --image=curlimages/curl --rm -it --restart=Never -- curl -sSI http://10.108.206.205

If you need external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP (internal-only). If you want to reach it from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on a node port (easiest, works anywhere).
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it (cloud or MetalLB).
  - Ingress: if you have an ingress controller and want host/path routing.
Tell me which you prefer and I can set it up.

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels. Service web/nginx had selector app=web, while the nginx Deployment/Pod is labeled app=nginx. This left the Service with no endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach the Pod.

What I changed
- Updated the Service selector to app=nginx.
- Result: Endpoints are now populated: nginx → 10.244.0.25:8080, and the Pod is Ready (1/1).

Current state
- Service: ClusterIP 10.108.206.205:80, selector app=nginx, targetPort 8080.
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.25:8080 (healthy).
- This should now be accessible from inside the cluster.

How to verify (inside the cluster)
- From another pod:
  - kubectl -n web run curl --image=curlimages/curl --rm -it --restart=Never -- curl -sSI http://nginx
- Or by ClusterIP:
  - kubectl -n web run curl --image=curlimages/curl --rm -it --restart=Never -- curl -sSI http://10.108.206.205

If you need external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP (internal-only). If you want to reach it from outside the cluster, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on a node port (easiest, works anywhere).
  - LoadBalancer: if your cluster supports it (cloud or MetalLB).
  - Ingress: if you have an ingress controller and want host/path routing.
Tell me which you prefer and I can set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and fixed.

Root cause
- Your Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
- No cluster node had that label, so the pods were Unschedulable (events: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”).
- With no pods, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local resulted in “connection refused.”

What I changed
- Labeled the node mcp-eval-cluster with environment=production-gpu to satisfy the Deployment’s nodeSelector.

Current state (verified)
- Pods are now running:
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-gs4kk 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-hd78h 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints are populated:
  - web-app-service -> 10.244.0.27:80, 10.244.0.28:80

This should clear the “connection refused” errors as traffic can now reach the backing pods.

Recommendations
- If the GPU/production pinning was unintentional, I can remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment instead of labeling nodes. Say the word and I’ll update the Deployment to be schedulable on any node.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe to the container (port 80) so the Service routes traffic only when the app is actually ready.

Want me to remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment (and optionally add a readiness probe)?

apiVersion: apps/v1

metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      restartPolicy: Always
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 25%
      maxSurge: 25%
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Here’s what I found and fixed.

Root cause
- Your Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
- No cluster node had that label, so the pods were Unschedulable (events: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”).
- With no pods, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local resulted in “connection refused.”

What I changed
- Labeled the node mcp-eval-cluster with environment=production-gpu to satisfy the Deployment’s nodeSelector.

Current state (verified)
- Pods are now running:
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-gs4kk 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-hd78h 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints are populated:
  - web-app-service -> 10.244.0.27:80, 10.244.0.28:80

This should clear the “connection refused” errors as traffic can now reach the backing pods.

Recommendations
- If the GPU/production pinning was unintentional, I can remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment instead of labeling nodes. Say the word and I’ll update the Deployment to be schedulable on any node.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe to the container (port 80) so the Service routes traffic only when the app is actually ready.

Want me to remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment (and optionally add a readiness probe)?

rawInput.resource:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      restartPolicy: Always
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 25%
      maxSurge: 25%
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600

rawInput.resource:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app-deployment
  namespace: webshop-frontend
  labels:
    app: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-app-container
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        imagePullPolicy: Always
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP
      restartPolicy: Always
      dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 25%
      maxSurge: 25%
  revisionHistoryLimit: 10
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 600

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found and fixed.

Root cause
- Your Deployment had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu.
- No cluster node had that label, so the pods were Unschedulable (events: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”).
- With no pods, the Service web-app-service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local resulted in “connection refused.”

What I changed
- Labeled the node mcp-eval-cluster with environment=production-gpu to satisfy the Deployment’s nodeSelector.

Current state (verified)
- Pods are now running:
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-gs4kk 1/1 Running
  - web-app-deployment-5d7bb895c8-hd78h 1/1 Running
- Service endpoints are populated:
  - web-app-service -> 10.244.0.27:80, 10.244.0.28:80

This should clear the “connection refused” errors as traffic can now reach the backing pods.

Recommendations
- If the GPU/production pinning was unintentional, I can remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment instead of labeling nodes. Say the word and I’ll update the Deployment to be schedulable on any node.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe to the container (port 80) so the Service routes traffic only when the app is actually ready.

Want me to remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment (and optionally add a readiness probe)?

Steps.message:
Done.

- Namespace: multi-container-logging (exists)
- Pod: communication-pod
- Containers (both under spec.containers):
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
    - Port 8080 exposed
    - Readiness probe: HTTP GET / on port 8080 (pod considered ready when web server serves traffic)
  - logger: busybox:latest
    - Command: sh -c "tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log"
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir)
- Mounts: both containers mount logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
- Additional: fsGroup set to 101 so nginx can write logs to the shared volume

Current status: Pod is Running and Ready.

Optional checks:
- View web-server readiness: kubectl get pod communication-pod -n multi-container-logging
- Watch processed logs: kubectl logs communication-pod -n multi-container-logging -c logger -f
- Test traffic locally: kubectl port-forward pod/communication-pod -n multi-container-logging 8080:8080 and curl http://localhost:8080/

  name: communication-pod
  namespace: multi-container-logging

  securityContext:
    fsGroup: 101
  volumes:
  - name: logs-volume
    emptyDir: {}
  containers:
  - name: web-server

    ports:

      name: http
      protocol: TCP

        path: /
        port: 8080
      initialDelaySeconds: 2
      periodSeconds: 5
      failureThreshold: 3

    image: busybox:latest
    imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
    command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -F /var/log/nginx/access.log"]
    volumeMounts:
    - name: logs-volume
      mountPath: /var/log/nginx

All requested namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies have been created and applied. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev, role=dev, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: env=dev, role=shared, shared=true
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

2) RBAC
- Each developer has full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding developer-admin in each dev-<name> namespace binding:
    - kind: User: <name>
    - kind: ServiceAccount: <name>-sa (in their namespace)
    - roleRef: ClusterRole admin
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - kind: User: alice, bob, charlie
    - kind: ServiceAccount: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
    - roleRef: ClusterRole view
- staging/prod are accessible only to cluster admins (no developer RoleBindings were created there; access is by your existing cluster-admin binding only)
- Service accounts created:
  - alice-sa in dev-alice
  - bob-sa in dev-bob
  - charlie-sa in dev-charlie

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu 4, memory 8Gi, pods 20, services 10
- staging/prod:
  - cpu 8, memory 16Gi, pods 50, services 20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in every non-system namespace: dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Intra-namespace allow:
  - allow-same-namespace in each namespace (enables pods to talk within the same namespace)
- DNS/system services:
  - allow-dns-egress in each namespace to kube-system:53 TCP/UDP (CoreDNS). This satisfies “Allow all namespaces to access DNS and system services” for DNS.
- Dev namespaces access:
  - Each dev namespace:
    - Egress allowed only to dev-shared (allow-egress-to-dev-shared)
    - Ingress allowed from dev-shared (allow-ingress-from-dev-shared)
  - dev-shared:
    - Ingress allowed from dev namespaces (env=dev, role=dev) and itself
    - Egress allowed to dev namespaces and itself
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic and DNS egress permitted; no traffic to/from any dev namespaces

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented default-deny network policies for all created namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod). No changes were made to system namespaces.

How to verify
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice  # should be no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice  # should be no
- ServiceAccount tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- Quotas:
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-alice -o yaml
- Network isolation (example from a test pod):
  - kubectl run -n dev-alice tmp --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -it -- rm -f tmp; wget -qO- http://svc-in-dev-bob  # should fail
  - From dev-alice to a service in dev-shared should succeed (once you create one)
  - DNS resolution test:
    - nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local 10.96.0.10 (or just nslookup kubernetes.default) from any namespace should succeed

Notes and optional adjustments
- If your DNS runs outside kube-system or under a different label, update the allow-dns-egress namespaceSelector accordingly.
- If pods need to reach the Kubernetes API server directly (beyond DNS), consider a targeted egress allow to the kubernetes.default service ClusterIP:443.
- For even stricter least privilege in dev namespaces, you could replace ClusterRole admin with edit (prevents RBAC/Quota changes by developers). You requested “full access,” so admin was used.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All requested namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies have been created and applied. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev, role=dev, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: env=dev, role=shared, shared=true
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

2) RBAC
- Each developer has full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding developer-admin in each dev-<name> namespace binding:
    - kind: User: <name>
    - kind: ServiceAccount: <name>-sa (in their namespace)
    - roleRef: ClusterRole admin
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - kind: User: alice, bob, charlie
    - kind: ServiceAccount: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
    - roleRef: ClusterRole view
- staging/prod are accessible only to cluster admins (no developer RoleBindings were created there; access is by your existing cluster-admin binding only)
- Service accounts created:
  - alice-sa in dev-alice
  - bob-sa in dev-bob
  - charlie-sa in dev-charlie

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu 4, memory 8Gi, pods 20, services 10
- staging/prod:
  - cpu 8, memory 16Gi, pods 50, services 20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in every non-system namespace: dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Intra-namespace allow:
  - allow-same-namespace in each namespace (enables pods to talk within the same namespace)
- DNS/system services:
  - allow-dns-egress in each namespace to kube-system:53 TCP/UDP (CoreDNS). This satisfies “Allow all namespaces to access DNS and system services” for DNS.
- Dev namespaces access:
  - Each dev namespace:
    - Egress allowed only to dev-shared (allow-egress-to-dev-shared)
    - Ingress allowed from dev-shared (allow-ingress-from-dev-shared)
  - dev-shared:
    - Ingress allowed from dev namespaces (env=dev, role=dev) and itself
    - Egress allowed to dev namespaces and itself
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic and DNS egress permitted; no traffic to/from any dev namespaces

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented default-deny network policies for all created namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod). No changes were made to system namespaces.

How to verify
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-bob --as alice  # should be no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice  # should be no
- ServiceAccount tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+):
  - kubectl -n dev-alice create token alice-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-bob create token bob-sa
  - kubectl -n dev-charlie create token charlie-sa
- Quotas:
  - kubectl get resourcequota -n dev-alice -o yaml
- Network isolation (example from a test pod):
  - kubectl run -n dev-alice tmp --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -it -- rm -f tmp; wget -qO- http://svc-in-dev-bob  # should fail
  - From dev-alice to a service in dev-shared should succeed (once you create one)
  - DNS resolution test:
    - nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local 10.96.0.10 (or just nslookup kubernetes.default) from any namespace should succeed

Notes and optional adjustments
- If your DNS runs outside kube-system or under a different label, update the allow-dns-egress namespaceSelector accordingly.
- If pods need to reach the Kubernetes API server directly (beyond DNS), consider a targeted egress allow to the kubernetes.default service ClusterIP:443.
- For even stricter least privilege in dev namespaces, you could replace ClusterRole admin with edit (prevents RBAC/Quota changes by developers). You requested “full access,” so admin was used.

If you want, I can generate a single consolidated YAML bundle reflecting all applied objects for your records.

outputSteps.content:
All requested namespaces, RBAC, quotas, and network policies have been created and applied. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets your requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Created: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Labels:
  - dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie: env=dev, role=dev, owner=<name>
  - dev-shared: env=dev, role=shared, shared=true
  - staging: env=staging
  - prod: env=prod

2) RBAC
- Each developer has full access to their own namespace:
  - RoleBinding developer-admin in each dev-<name> namespace binding:
    - kind: User: <name>
    - kind: ServiceAccount: <name>-sa (in their namespace)
    - roleRef: ClusterRole admin
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding devs-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - kind: User: alice, bob, charlie
    - kind: ServiceAccount: alice-sa (dev-alice), bob-sa (dev-bob), charlie-sa (dev-charlie)
    - roleRef: ClusterRole view
- staging/prod are accessible only to cluster admins (no developer RoleBindings were created there; access is by your existing cluster-admin binding only)
- Service accounts created:
  - alice-sa in dev-alice
  - bob-sa in dev-bob
  - charlie-sa in dev-charlie

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - requests.cpu=2, limits.cpu=2
  - requests.memory=4Gi, limits.memory=4Gi
  - pods=10, services=5
- dev-shared:
  - cpu 4, memory 8Gi, pods 20, services 10
- staging/prod:
  - cpu 8, memory 16Gi, pods 50, services 20

4) Network Policies and Isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in every non-system namespace: dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Intra-namespace allow:
  - allow-same-namespace in each namespace (enables pods to talk within the same namespace)
- DNS/system services:
  - allow-dns-egress in each namespace to kube-system:53 TCP/UDP (CoreDNS). This satisfies “Allow all namespaces to access DNS and system services” for DNS.
- Dev namespaces access:
  - Each dev namespace:
    - Egress allowed only to dev-shared (allow-egress-to-dev-shared)
    - Ingress allowed from dev-shared (allow-ingress-from-dev-shared)
  - dev-shared:
    - Ingress allowed from dev namespaces (env=dev, role=dev) and itself
    - Egress allowed to dev namespaces and itself
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - Only same-namespace traffic and DNS egress permitted; no traffic to/from any dev namespaces

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented default-deny network policies for all created namespaces (dev-*, dev-shared, staging, prod). No changes were made to system namespaces.

How to verify
- RBAC:
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-alice --as alice
  - kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n dev-alice --as alice

Done.

What I applied:
- Namespace statefulset-test
- Headless Service db (clusterIP: None) for stable identities
- StatefulSet db with:
  - replicas: 3
  - volumeClaimTemplates: 1Gi RWO per pod, mounted at /data
  - initContainer that writes initial_data to /data/test
  - busybox:1.36 main container (sleep infinity)

Then I scaled the StatefulSet back down to 1 replica.

Notes:
- After scaling to 1, only pod db-0 remains running. PVCs are retained by default on scale-down, so you will still have:
  - data-db-0 (bound to db-0)
  - data-db-1 and data-db-2 (retained; not mounted to any pod)

Verify the data:
- kubectl -n statefulset-test exec -it db-0 -- sh -c 'cat /data/test' 
  Expected output: initial_data

If you’d like me to also verify pod readiness or clean up the retained PVCs for db-1/db-2, tell me and I’ll proceed.

outputSteps.content:
I tried to inspect the Argo CD Application misconfigured-app in namespace argocd-eval-fix-proj, but the cluster reports that the Argo CD CRDs are not installed:

- No matches for kind "Application" in version "argoproj.io/v1alpha1"
- The CRDs applications.argoproj.io and appprojects.argoproj.io are not found

Because the CRDs are missing, I cannot:
- Read the Application to see which project it references, nor
- Create the corresponding AppProject (the API server doesn’t recognize that kind)

What I need to proceed
- Either install Argo CD CRDs in the cluster (so I can read the Application and create the AppProject), or
- Provide the Application manifest (or at least these fields):
  - spec.project (the project name to create)
  - spec.source.repoURL (to set spec.sourceRepos)
  - spec.destination.server and spec.destination.namespace (to set spec.destinations)

If you can share those values now, I’ll create the AppProject immediately. For reference, the AppProject I will create will look like:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AppProject
metadata:
  name: <spec.project from Application>
  namespace: argocd-eval-fix-proj
spec:
  sourceRepos:
    - <spec.source.repoURL from Application>
  destinations:
    - server: <spec.destination.server from Application>
      namespace: <spec.destination.namespace from Application>

Optionally, I can make it permissive (sourceRepos: ["*"], destinations: [{server: "*", namespace: "*"}]) if you prefer until we can tighten it, but I still need the project name the Application references.

I created the required namespaces:
- argocd-eval-full-setup (for Argo CD control plane and CRs)
- team-x (target namespace for your app)

However, creating these three Argo CD resources failed because the cluster does not have the Argo CD CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs) installed:
- ArgoCD (argoproj.io/v1beta1, kind ArgoCD)
- AppProject (argoproj.io/v1alpha1)
- Application (argoproj.io/v1alpha1)

I also checked for Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM)/OpenShift operator resources, but they’re not available on this cluster, so we can’t install the Argo CD Operator via Subscription/OperatorGroup.

How would you like to proceed? Two workable options:

Option A — Upstream Argo CD install (no operator)
- I install Argo CD core components (controller, repo-server, server, redis, CRDs) directly into argocd-eval-full-setup using the official manifests.
- This will create the Application and AppProject CRDs.
- Then I’ll create:
  - AppProject team-x-project (source: https://github.com/team-x/apps, dest: namespace team-x, server https://kubernetes.default.svc)
  - Application team-x-api (repo https://github.com/team-x/apps, path api/, project team-x-project, dest team-x)
- Note: This path does not provide an ArgoCD (kind ArgoCD) instance, because that CRD exists only with the operator. Functionally, you’ll still get a complete, working Argo CD.

Option B — Install the Argo CD Operator (argocd-operator) manually
- I apply the operator’s CRDs, RBAC, and controller Deployment (no OLM required).
- Then I create the ArgoCD (kind ArgoCD) instance argocd-team-x in argocd-eval-full-setup.
- After the operator brings up Argo CD, I’ll create the AppProject and Application as requested.
- This exactly matches your requested kinds and versions, but requires me to apply the operator’s (fairly large) manifests.

Please confirm which option you prefer:
- A: Upstream Argo CD (simpler, faster; no ArgoCD kind)
- B: Argo CD Operator (matches your ArgoCD kind; more manifests)

Also let me know if you want:
- Application auto-sync enabled (I can set syncPolicy.automated with prune/selfHeal).
- Any specific Argo CD version or container registry mirrors/proxies.

I created the required namespaces:
- argocd-eval-full-setup (for Argo CD control plane and CRs)
- team-x (target namespace for your app)

However, creating these three Argo CD resources failed because the cluster does not have the Argo CD CustomResourceDefinitions (CRDs) installed:
- ArgoCD (argoproj.io/v1beta1, kind ArgoCD)
- AppProject (argoproj.io/v1alpha1)
- Application (argoproj.io/v1alpha1)

I also checked for Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM)/OpenShift operator resources, but they’re not available on this cluster, so we can’t install the Argo CD Operator via Subscription/OperatorGroup.

How would you like to proceed? Two workable options:

Option A — Upstream Argo CD install (no operator)
- I install Argo CD core components (controller, repo-server, server, redis, CRDs) directly into argocd-eval-full-setup using the official manifests.
- This will create the Application and AppProject CRDs.
- Then I’ll create:
  - AppProject team-x-project (source: https://github.com/team-x/apps, dest: namespace team-x, server https://kubernetes.default.svc)
  - Application team-x-api (repo https://github.com/team-x/apps, path api/, project team-x-project, dest team-x)
- Note: This path does not provide an ArgoCD (kind ArgoCD) instance, because that CRD exists only with the operator. Functionally, you’ll still get a complete, working Argo CD.

Option B — Install the Argo CD Operator (argocd-operator) manually
- I apply the operator’s CRDs, RBAC, and controller Deployment (no OLM required).
- Then I create the ArgoCD (kind ArgoCD) instance argocd-team-x in argocd-eval-full-setup.
- After the operator brings up Argo CD, I’ll create the AppProject and Application as requested.
- This exactly matches your requested kinds and versions, but requires me to apply the operator’s (fairly large) manifests.

Please confirm which option you prefer:
- A: Upstream Argo CD (simpler, faster; no ArgoCD kind)
- B: Argo CD Operator (matches your ArgoCD kind; more manifests)

Also let me know if you want:
- Application auto-sync enabled (I can set syncPolicy.automated with prune/selfHeal).
- Any specific Argo CD version or container registry mirrors/proxies.
